newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Cotton seen easing in Pakistan, firming in India.
newsitem.headline: Cotton seen easing in Pakistan, firming in India.

text.p: Cotton prices are likely to fall in Pakistan due to an overhang of unsold stocks but may gain slightly in India, dealers said on Friday.
In Pakistan, dealers said demand was low this week with mill owners short of funds and international yarn prices depressed. Most deals were done on credit.
"Depressed yarn sales remain the key reason for mill owners' liquidity problem," said dealer Khushi Ram.
"Cotton rates will slide in the coming weeks as there are still piles of unsold cotton stocks with the ginners, while supplies from the new crop (1997/98) are due to start in June."

The state-run Cotton Export Corporation of Pakistan said cotton output in 1996/97 (July-June) had reached 8.73 million 375-lb bales by Thursday, compared to 9.93 million in the year-ago period. It said ginners held 1.508 million bales.
"There are expectations that the 1997/98 crop will be better than the previous year because the area under cotton cultivation has increased," Ram said.
In the kerb market, NIAB-78 traded at 1,900 ($47.09) to 2,100 rupees per maund (37.32 kg).
Karachi Cotton Association spot rates in rupees per maund including 10 percent sales tax (Pakistani markets were closed on April 18 due to Eid al-Adha holidays):
Friday April 16 (Wednesday)

In India, prices were subdued this week might gain marginally in the next week or two. Demand for cotton from yarn mills had been dull due to a downtrend in world prices though the trend was slightly better in the last few days.
"Prices are likely to firm in the next few days but towards end-May and early June prices may fall as pre-monsoon rains may force farmers and merchants to sell stocks," one trader said.
Most farmers and merchants sell stocks at this time to avoid rain damage.

Political uncertainty in the past few days, culminating in a parliamentary confidence vote on Monday in support of a new government headed by Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral also kept the market under pressure, traders said.
"The political dust has yet to settle," said a trader. "A proper government is needed to take decisions on exports and other crucial issues."

Bengal Deshi was steady around 890/950 rupees per maund (37.32 kg). Gujarat Kalyan (medium staple) was unchanged at 13,200 rupees per candy (355.56 kg). Gujarat Wagad was steady at 12,600 per candy. Gujarat Sankar-4 gained 500 rupees to 16,500/17,000 per candy.
($1 = 40.34 Pakistani rupees)
